prompt: Compute the Levenshtein edit distance between two strings and then reconstruct one shortest list of KEEP / SUB / DEL / INS steps under a fixed tie-break rule. Complete distance and editScript in the starter file, then run the tests.
starterCode:
/**
 * TASK: Compute the edit distance between two strings AND reconstruct the edits.
 *
 * distance(source, target) returns the Levenshtein distance: the smallest number of
 * single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions that turn source into target.
 * distance("kitten", "sitting") is 3.
 *
 * editScript(source, target) returns one shortest sequence of steps as a String,
 * with the steps separated by "; " (semicolon then one space). The four step formats are:
 *
 *   KEEP c     the character c is the same in both and is left alone (costs 0)
 *   SUB a>b    the character a in source becomes b in target (costs 1)
 *   DEL a      the character a in source is removed (costs 1)
 *   INS b      the character b from target is added (costs 1)
 *
 * Example: editScript("cat", "cart") -> "KEEP c; KEEP a; INS r; KEEP t"
 *          editScript("ab", "")      -> "DEL a; DEL b"
 *          editScript("", "")        -> ""            (empty string, no steps)
 *
 * There can be several shortest scripts, so the tie-break is fixed and you MUST follow
 * it. Walk forward from the start of both strings; at each position, of the choices that
 * still lead to a shortest script, take the FIRST one from this list:
 *
 *   1. KEEP or SUB  (consume one character from each string)
 *   2. DEL          (consume one character from source)
 *   3. INS          (consume one character from target)
 *
 * With that rule editScript("ab", "ba") is "SUB a>b; SUB b>a", not "DEL a; KEEP b; INS a".
 *
 * Edge cases the tests check: either argument may be empty. Treat a null argument as the
 * empty string in both methods.

explanation: Filling the distance table is the classic dynamic program: dist[i][j], the distance between the two suffixes starting at i and j, is the cheapest of substituting (cost 0 when the characters match), deleting, or inserting. Reconstruction reuses that same table: standing at (i, j), a move is part of some shortest script exactly when its cost plus the distance it leads to equals dist[i][j], and the tie-break just says which of those legal moves to prefer. Because the table is built from the ends backwards, the walk can go forward from (0, 0) and emit the steps in reading order with no reversal.
hints: Define dist[i][j] as the distance between source.substring(i) and target.substring(j). Then dist[m][j] = target.length() - j and dist[i][n] = source.length() - i, and the rest is filled by looping i and j downwards.
To reconstruct, do not store back-pointers -- re-derive them. The diagonal move is allowed exactly when dist[i][j] == cost + dist[i+1][j+1], and the deletion when dist[i][j] == 1 + dist[i+1][j].
Test the three moves in the order the Javadoc gives (diagonal, then delete, then insert) and take the first one that is allowed. Also guard i and j against running off the end of either string.
